> "I think they're trying to get ahead of the bubble possibly bursting,"

And while Wall Street's Dan Ives is confident the IPO will be a success, he says the company has not yet produced the sort of numbers that would justify its current valuation. [...] Companies are no different. They ask share investors (equity) and lenders (debt) for cash to operate.

The big difference is that firms will look to finance investments for future growth.

Investors, naturally, want to know they will not just get their money back but also have their investment grow over time.

The S-1 filing that tees up the IPO flagged what Anthropic sees as the risks from AI — and to its business model. Among them are the risk that its AI models could develop faster than the company can keep them safe, or that they could be used to cause harm — or take harmful actions on their own. It also flagged the risk of heightened scrutiny or political backlash for the company's views on policy and regulation. [...] Anthropic filed final paperwork with regulators on Monday for an IPO under the ticker symbol ANT that reports have said could value the company at between $1.5 trillion to $2 trillion.

That would put it in league with Elon Musk's rocketry and AI company SpaceX, which was valued at around $1.8 trillion when it listed in June. Anthropic's listing prospectus did not say how many shares the company will offer or at what price range. [...] But, he added, "there's concern that we may be in an AI bubble. We're in a very dynamic industry, to say the least, and we can expect a lot of volatility in the markets." Still, Angel said, it makes sense for Anthropic to "strike while the iron is hot" and list shares now to get as high a valuation as possible.

-- San Francisco-based artificial intelligence company Anthropic has filed for an initial public offering, a move expected to inject billions of dollars into the city's economy and potentially intensify pressure on an already competitive housing market.

The IPO is projected to be one of the largest in history. Ted Egan, chief economist for the City and County of San Francisco, said the company's value could reach extraordinary levels.

"Potentially worth $2 trillion dollars," Egan said. [...] "I think it's easier for our city and state and federal leaders to demonize the software engineers than to take a look at themselves and the laws that they perpetuated for multiple generations in San Francisco," he said.

Anthropic is not the only major artificial intelligence company drawing attention in San Francisco. OpenAI, which is based in the city, is projected to be the next local company to pursue an IPO and is valued at $1.2 trillion. [...] City officials are preparing for the economic impact that could follow. Egan said San Francisco experienced a similar, though much smaller, wave of wealth creation when Uber went public in 2019 with an initial valuation of about $82 billion. He said the city expects increased revenue through property and sales taxes as Anthropic employees gain access to their wealth.

items.title: VPA Report Outlines 34 Ways to Tax Artificial Intelligence | Vanderbilt Law School | Vanderbilt University
items.snippet: The 34 options reach different parts of this stack and fall into six categories,...
items.raw_snippet: The 34 options reach different parts of this stack and fall into six categories, largely by who would nominally pay each tax, though many could pass costs on to others: (1) data center taxes, (2) chip taxes, and (3) data taxes, which focus on the key inputs necessary for AI; (4) AI company and product taxes; (5) automation taxes; and (6) general tax reforms relevant to AI. [...] The report categorizes AI taxes—taxes that reach AI products, the inputs AI depends on, or those profiting from AI—by analyzing money flows through what’s commonly called the AI Tech Stack: employers pay application developers, who pay AI model providers for models trained on data created by others and private information; model providers pay compute providers, which build data centers and buy chips, energy, land, and other infrastructure. Financiers invest billions across this stack. [...] “Our current AI boom is partially funded by sales and use tax exemptions, property tax abatements, bonus depreciation, preferential tax treatment for investors, and rules that favor capital over wages,” said Ramzanali. “While AI contributes little to the tax base today, policymakers can change this reality. From city councils to Congress, taxing AI is starting to become a priority, and policymakers should consider and weigh a full range of options to tax AI.”
